records.title: Emerging Perspectives From the Hearing Voices Movement: Implications for Research and Practice
records.abstract: The international Hearing Voices Movement (HVM) is a prominent mental health service-user/survivor movement that promotes the needs and perspectives of experts by experience in the phenomenon of hearing voices (auditory verbal hallucinations). The main tenet of the HVM is the notion that hearing voices is a meaningful human experience, and in this article, we discuss the historical growth and influence of the HVM before considering the implications of its values for research and practice in relation to voice-hearing. Among other recommendations, we suggest that the involvement of voice-hearers in research and a greater use of narrative and qualitative approaches are essential. Challenges for implementing user-led research are identified, and avenues for future developments are discussed.

records.title: Hearing Voices Sessions in Providing Peer Support: A First-Person Account and Voice Hearer’s Perspective
records.abstract: This paper describes hearing voices sessions as part of providing peer support in a men’s psychiatric acute unit. The intertwining of process (a service user and first-person account) and subject (hearing voices sessions in peer support) leads to greater insight into hearing voices in mental health. The methods involved the peer support worker keeping a reflective journal of experiences and interactions on the ward and participant observation. These methods allow a first-person and service user perspective as well as a hidden narrative on the experience of voice hearing. Hearing voices sessions and peer support offer emotional and practical help. They provide better insight into the experience of hearing voices, seeing things, and strange or unusual thoughts and beliefs. There is reciprocity and mutuality in the hearing voices sessions, which results in better experiences and satisfaction with care as well as feelings of safety and hope of recovery. The voice(s) is/are mapped so they can be better understood and coped with by the voice hearer. There is an abundance of research and literature on both peer support in mental health and talking-based therapies for voice hearing. However, there is little on these topics from a service user’s perspective, which is rarer, so this account is quite unique. Ben has a diagnosis of schizophrenia and is a voice hearer. I have mainly heard voices of a demonic and hellish nature, saying things like: “You wait until you see what I’m going to do to you!!,” “Hot fire in your eyes,” and “On the bonfire with him.” For over 2 years, I was in and out of hospital and felt excluded, stigmatized, confused, threatened, and frightened. I felt left behind in general life, by health and social care services, and by being unemployed. I withdrew into myself and felt zombified by the adverse effects of antipsychotic medication. I felt like a shell, living a half-life and unvalued. My experiences, and the experiences of other people with mental illness, emphasize the point of needing to involve people, in all aspects of life, health and social care services, education, and in employment such as running hearing voices sessions as part of peer support. Peer support involves emotional and practical support in mental health. It draws on the lived and personal experience and insight of peer support workers in their interactions with people with mental health problems. It is important to share experiences and stories in a hope-filled, positive, and empathetic manner that opens a gateway to people’s common humanity so as to overcome the challenges of mental health. Peer support is when people use their own lived experiences to help each other. People share common concerns and draw on their own lived experiences to offer emotional and practical support to help each other move forwards in a journey of recovery. According to Repper: It is through this trusting relationship, which offers companionship, empathy and empowerment, that feelings of isolation and rejection can be replaced with hope, a sense of agency and belief in personal control (Repper, 2013, p. 4)1 In the view of Ben, you get back what you give to other people: such as support, care, kindness, and even a bit of love. As part of peer support, this paper finds that it is important to engage people in hearing voices sessions and discussions about the experience of hearing voices, seeing things (hallucinations), and strange beliefs/ thoughts (delusions). This leads to more insight into psychosis. The activity of just listening to people’s experiences of psychosis is found in this paper to be a therapeutic one. Ben led on hearing voices sessions as he has lived experience of schizophrenia, psychosis, and voices. At the Recovery Champions course, people engage in “voice mapping.” Recovery coaches (in the present case peer support workers) talk to the person about the voice(s). For example: its gender (is it male/female/trans/non-binary/other)? Its age? Does it whisper or shout? Is it positive or negative? Is it one voice or many? Does it advise or is it commanding? Is it like an echo? What the voice actually says? Does it occur at certain times of the day? How is the voice triggered (eg, by stress/anxiety)? The voice is therefore mapped so it can be better understood and coped with by the voice hearer (see: https://workingtorecovery.co.uk). Hearing voices sessions should not be longer than 20–30 min so as not to pressurize or overwhelm people and can be run individually or in a group. The findings are based on Ben’s reflective journal and participant observation on the ward. The most salient and pertinent findings are summarized in this section and linked to ImROC’s core values/principles of peer support work (see Repper1). It is important to establish connection, mutuality, and reciprocity at the earliest possible stage with people with mental health problems. In the first week, I opened up in a hearing voices session and told a group of 8 people my story of mental illness and hearing voices. I described the hellish and demonic quality of my voices and what they said. For example, in a whisper: “You’re a swimmer, Ben.” And then, shouting: “Boiling water!.” “You hear voices as well,” they said in a positive, sharing, and appreciative manner. It is important to share lived experience and coping strategies. A group of 6 people asked me how I coped with my voices: “You need to listen to what people are saying,” I responded. They thought this a good idea and agreed. I explained the balance needed in getting the medication right, the involvement of family and carers, and the therapeutic value of ward activities and engaging with staff in their recovery journey. Hearing voices sessions must promote feelings of safety. I noticed the panic of staff and distress of people on the ward when the alarms sounded, which was frequently. In hearing voices sessions people said the alarms made their voices and psychosis worse because of the stress and anxiety. I asked people how the alarms made them feel. Comments include: “I think they’re coming for me,” “It makes me frightened,” “It makes me cry,” “I want the alarm to end,” “It’s anxiety,” “It’s about to kick off,” “I need to stay out the way,” “I feel numb,” “It makes my headache,” and “I feel like screaming.” One person said: “It doesn’t bother me. I feel nothing,” so feelings about the alarms are inherently subjective. A pocket buzzer alarm, perhaps an App or traffic light system might help calm the ward, diminish people’s voices, and promote feelings of safety. The traffic light system might involve: Red (Suicide attempt or severe aggression/violence), Amber (Early warning signs of these), and Green (All clear and safe on the ward). Safety also involves facilitating feelings of belonging and mutual support among people with mental health problems themselves. I did a hearing voices session with someone who hears both male and female voices of a spiritual nature and believes other people can see through his eyes. He said he was ignoring his voices and that talking with me had reassured him that his experiences are common among people with schizophrenia. This was his first episode of psychosis. I said that other people with mental health problems on the ward would look after him. “We’ll look after you,” said a healthcare assistant and others sitting nearby. Hearing voices sessions also have to be progressive in steps to recovery. One person initially talked about his voices and thoughts that people want to kill and torture him and his family, so I engaged in a hearing voices session and listened and reassured him. This promoted feelings of calm, being heard, and well-being. He said: “The staff don’t talk to me as I say the same things again and again,” (about being persecuted). And then: “Thank you for listening to me.” Later on, I asked him how he coped in the past. He said a psychologist had helped improve his mental state. I then helped him to write notes for his ward review to formally request psychological/talking therapies and some days later he was given and engaging in group psychological therapy. It is important to connect with and understand people’s lived experience perspective of mental illness. This means not making assumptions about people’s psychosis, hallucinations, and delusions. For example, I heard staff discussing a black and minority ethnic person who thinks he is Jesus Christ and they classified this experience as a delusion. In a hearing voices session, I asked the person why he thought he was Jesus Christ. He said: “I have to fight demons and my voices. I have to help people.” He continued: “I feel like I’m being crucified by my demons and voices.” Others sitting nearby agreed: “It is like being crucified!.” This shows that his/their delusion was real to him/them and symbolic of the pain and suffering associated with schizophrenia. People’s voices are often of a religious nature and involve demonic voices, sometimes telling them to hurt themselves or other people and being derogatory about the voice hearer as well as staff. Over the past months, about a dozen people have said that they hear voices that they are in or going to hell. I told them all what Winston Churchill said about his “black dog” of depression: “If you’re going through hell, keep going.” I also said: “We won’t let them get you!.” People running hearing voices sessions also need to be curious and non-stigmatizing. I had an intriguing hearing voices session with someone who hears voices, but these are like echoes. The voice would repeat the individual’s thoughts and words but in a sinister, angry, and horrible manner. I had never heard of this before so I was very curious (not afraid, disconcerted, or stigmatizing). The person said that the voice was worse after lunch, so I have been checking with him at this time to further discuss the voice as well as to promote feelings of care and safety. Hearing voices sessions also need to be trauma informed and can sometimes involve very distressing and unsettling stories and experiences of mental illness. I spoke to someone who hears voices commanding him to spit out and vomit his food and liquids. This often occurs after medication has been dispensed just after lunchtime. This lowers the level of antipsychotic medication so the person becomes quite psychotic. In a hearing voices session, we discussed why this was the case. The person was wary at first. But after 3 sessions it emerged that the individual had experienced childhood trauma. His father was coercive and controlling and there was domestic violence by the father on the person’s mother. The person eventually disclosed that the mother would hit him as a child on the hand with a tin opener in the kitchen. This was a latent memory so the hearing voices session revealed why the person felt compelled to obey the voices to spit out or vomit his food. I then fetched food and drinks for the person from the canteen, as he was claustrophobic and felt unsafe in this situation. Finally, it is crucial to put the person with mental health problems first and to be nondirective. I took someone on escorted leave and he described his vivid nightmares and voices, which seemed real, and his fears that he is going to hell. He gets little sleep. He also sees people: “Marie,” who is a sweet 15-year-old girl but does not age. She was sitting next to an older man, her father, on a bench nearby. He said that he feels betrayed and abandoned by friends. He asked me if his frightening experiences were real. Although I think they are real for the person experiencing them, I had to tread gently and put him first. “They’re not real,” I said. “Promise?,” he responded. “I promise,” I said. Sharing stories, hidden narratives, and experiences of hearing voices with people leads to trust, feelings of being valued, heard, and accepted. It results in better experiences of care and being seen as a person first (and not just someone labeled with mental illness). Peer support work and hearing voices sessions offer hope of recovery and feelings of safety in an inpatient environment that can sometimes be experienced as distressing, frightening, lethargic, boring, and even hostile. Hearing voices sessions promote insight via the discussion of hearing voices and seeing things (hallucinations) as well as having unusual/strange thoughts and beliefs (delusions). People’s experiences of psychosis are often silenced, ignored, and vetoed by psychiatry, mental health nursing, and by healthcare assistants. They are considered unreal, shameful, sometimes bizarre, and disturbing, even though they are real to the person experiencing them. But not by peer support workers. While talking therapies and psychological interventions facilitate discussion about hallucinations and delusions, hearing voices sessions draw on the shared lived experience of both the peer support worker and person with mental health problems. This provides shared insight and understanding into hallucinations and delusions. For example, the voice is mapped and laid bare so it can be better understood. The act of just listening about hallucinations and delusions is found in this paper to be in itself a therapeutic one. Escorted leave (individual) is a particularly good situation and context in which to discuss sensitive and confidential issues. Hearing voices sessions are also conducted between equals rather than professional/expert and service user/client. Running hearing voices sessions is therapeutic for both the peer support worker and person(s) with mental health problems. Helping someone to map their voices through shared insight induces feelings of altruism, making a difference, and connecting with another human being in their recovery journey. Hearing voices sessions in peer support do not diagnose, intervene, or treat with medication. It provides a safe and nonjudgmental space free from fear and recrimination. People’s voices are treated as real to the person(s) experiencing psychosis, as are seeing things and strange thoughts or beliefs. Hearing voices sessions open a reciprocal and mutual space to better understand voices and treat them as valid and meaningful to the person experiencing psychosis. It is important to note that hearing voices sessions are best done with only 1 member of staff/ voices coach/peer supporter. Ben recently had new peer support workers shadowing him and people are less forthcoming and interactive about their voices in this situation. Hearing voices sessions are best in a one-to-one format or dyad. People with mental health problems are less forthcoming when talking with more than 1 member of staff as well as staff who are non-voice hearers. The authors would like to thank the peer support team and other colleagues. Many thanks to Renee, Rosario, Charlotte, Olivia, Liz, and Lauren. The authors have declared that there are no conflicts of interest in relation to the subject of this study.

records.title: T161. HEARING VOICES AMONG INDIGENOUS MAASAI WOMEN IN TANZANIA: IMPLICATIONS FOR GLOBAL MENTAL HEALTH
records.abstract: Studies of the health of indigenous and tribal people can shed light on health inequalities with implications for global mental health. Almost no previous studies of mental health among the Maasai in Kenya or Tanzania or even pastoralist groups in general are available, with the exception of one mentioning the stress of rural-to-urban migration. While engaged in ethnographic research in 2013, Myers interviewed 13 Maasai women in northern Tanzania about their everyday lives. Interested in the phenomenology of voice-hearing, she also asked them if they heard voices. Eleven of the women (85%) reported regularly hearing voices that they found to be distressing. Myers returned in 2015 to collect data from a larger sample, which has resulted in this report. For this study, we used a convenience sample (n=73) of females taken from a broader study whose eligibility criteria included being a Maasai person living in the Arusha Region of Tanzania and over the age of 18. We excluded people who reported being psychiatric patients or family members of patients being seen by the local mental health coordinator to create a nonclinical community sample. This project conducted an initial survey to: 1) estimate the community prevalence of voice-hearing, or auditory verbal hallucinations (AVHs) in this specific population; and, 2) examine any demographic correlates and two specific hypothesized correlates based on previous literature about voice-hearing (e.g., psychological stress and potentially traumatic events). The prevalence of AVHs in this community sample was quite high compared to other studies in sub-Saharan Africa, at 34.3%. There were no differences between participants who did and did not experience AVHs in terms of demographics, but those experiencing AVHs had a statistically significantly higher level of psychological distress (30.1, SD=6.0, compared to 25.1, SD=6.0), with a Cohen’s d effect size of .87. Even though a numerical difference was observed in terms of potentially traumatic events (4.6, SD=2.1, compared to 3.8, SD=2.3), this difference was not statistically significant (d=.38). Hearing distressing voices may be an indicator of mental ill health that is easily recognizable to community health workers and brings much-needed attention to communities in need. Maasai women face tremendous social adversity in this time of rapid social, economic, and climate change in the region. Evidence for a link between stressful life events, social disadvantage, and the development of psychotic symptoms is strong in Europe, but not as well-developed in this region. The high level of psychosocial stress and AVHs in our sample may also be indicative of extreme social adversity. Maasai women have been historically disenfranchised since the advent of colonial and postcolonial policies favoring men. Women in this region also experiences extreme states of deprivation, including a 21.5 year gap in life expectancy at birth compared to the local population (for all Maasai), 81% severe food insecurity, and a rate of 59% for the stunted growth of children (as compared to their neighbors, the Meru, with 21% of children with stunted growth). Due to local livelihood insecurity, the age of first marriage has been decreasing, resulting in increased pressure on women. This analysis contextualizes these findings and calls for further research on the epidemiology of voice-hearing in this region, as well as further work on the phenomenology of these AVHs so that we can best understand how to address them and improve mental health outcomes for this marginalized group.

records.title: Varieties of Voice-Hearing: Psychics and the Psychosis Continuum
records.abstract: Hearing voices that are not present is a prominent symptom of serious mental illness. However, these experiences may be common in the non-help-seeking population, leading some to propose the existence of a continuum of psychosis from health to disease. Thus far, research on this continuum has focused on what is impaired in help-seeking groups. Here we focus on protective factors in non-help-seeking voice-hearers. We introduce a new study population: clairaudient psychics who receive daily auditory messages. We conducted phenomenological interviews with these subjects, as well as with patients diagnosed with a psychotic disorder who hear voices, people with a diagnosis of a psychotic disorder who do not hear voices, and matched control subjects (without voices or a diagnosis). We found the hallucinatory experiences of psychic voice-hearers to be very similar to those of patients who were diagnosed. We employed techniques from forensic psychiatry to conclude that the psychics were not malingering. Critically, we found that this sample of non-help-seeking voice hearers were able to control the onset and offset of their voices, that they were less distressed by their voice-hearing experiences and that, the first time they admitted to voice-hearing, the reception by others was much more likely to be positive. Patients had much more negative voice-hearing experiences, were more likely to receive a negative reaction when sharing their voices with others for the first time, and this was subsequently more disruptive to their social relationships. We predict that this sub-population of healthy voice-hearers may have much to teach us about the neurobiology, cognitive psychology and ultimately the treatment of voices that are distressing.
